clinicalPearls: Cervical ectropion is the presence of endocervical columnar epithelium everted onto the ectocervix around the external os, and it is a normal physiological finding rather than a true erosion.
It is common in high-oestrogen states such as adolescence, pregnancy and combined hormonal contraceptive use.
It appears as a red, velvety zone around the os because the thin single-layered columnar epithelium reveals the underlying vasculature.
Most are asymptomatic, but the fragile epithelium may produce postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding and a copious, non-offensive mucoid discharge.
It is benign and usually requires only reassurance, with no treatment needed.
Symptoms often settle once the hormonal stimulus is withdrawn, for example on stopping the combined pill, as squamous metaplasia re-covers the area.
Persistently troublesome symptoms can be treated by ablation such as cryotherapy or diathermy once other causes are excluded.
The transformation zone lies at the squamocolumnar junction within the ectropion and is the key site sampled during cervical screening.
reference.pathophysiology: Under oestrogenic influence the squamocolumnar junction migrates outward onto the ectocervix, exposing delicate endocervical columnar epithelium to the vaginal environment. Because this epithelium is a single vascular layer, it bleeds easily on contact and secretes abundant mucus, accounting for the typical symptoms. Over time the acidic vaginal pH induces squamous metaplasia that forms the transformation zone, and the junction eventually recedes; the process is neither inflammatory nor truly erosive despite the historical term erosion.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or early cervical carcinoma
Contact bleeding from another cervical or vaginal cause
additionalInvestigations: Speculum examination as the basis of clinical diagnosis
Cervical cytology and HPV testing in line with the screening programme
Colposcopy when cytology is abnormal or the lesion looks suspicious
Endocervical swabs for sexually transmitted infections where there is discharge or bleeding
Directed biopsy if there is any suspicion of neoplasia
redFlags: Abnormal cervical cytology or high-risk HPV positivity
An irregular, friable or contact-bleeding lesion suspicious for malignancy
Presentation in a postmenopausal woman, in whom an oestrogen-driven ectropion is unexpected
Associated infective symptoms that fail to resolve
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent as the condition is benign and frequently self-limiting, with symptoms resolving spontaneously or after simple ablative treatment, and it carries no malignant potential in itself.
pitfalls: Using the misleading term erosion, which can needlessly alarm the patient.
Attributing abnormal bleeding to ectropion without excluding cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, carcinoma and infection.
Ablating the cervix before excluding neoplasia and infection.
Overlooking chlamydial cervicitis, which can resemble an ectropion.
Performing unnecessary ablation during early pregnancy.
references: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Cervical screening and cervical ectropion
Llewellyn-Jones Fundamentals of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
management: Reassure the patient, as it is a benign physiological finding needing no treatment when asymptomatic
Remove the hormonal stimulus where relevant, since stopping or changing combined hormonal contraception often settles symptoms
Offer ablative treatment with cryotherapy or electrocautery for troublesome persistent contact bleeding or mucoid discharge
Ensure cervical cytology and HPV screening are up to date and exclude infection with endocervical swabs
Arrange colposcopy and directed biopsy if cytology is abnormal or the lesion looks suspicious
Refer to gynaecology if symptoms persist despite conservative measures
